section-2: The Universal Human Values course used in Indian colleges and universities follows the approach developed for the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE). Its main textbook is 'A Foundation Course in Human Values and Professional Ethics' by R.R. Gaur, R. Asthana and G.P. Bagaria. The approach draws on the philosophy of A. Nagraj (Madhyasth Darshan).

The course does not give a list of 'dos and don'ts'. It invites students to explore and verify values for themselves, so that values become their own understanding rather than rules imposed from outside.
section-5: The UHV approach gives guidelines for value education. It should be universal (applicable to all human beings regardless of caste, religion, nation or time), rational (based on reasoning, not blind belief), natural and verifiable (naturally acceptable and testable in one's own life), all-encompassing (covering all dimensions of life: thought, behaviour, work and realization) and leading to harmony (within oneself, with others and with nature).

Value education complements skill education. Skills tell us 'how to do' something, while values tell us 'what to do' and 'why'. Both are needed: values without skills cannot be put into practice, and skills without values can be harmful, as in the misuse of technology.
In Mizo society, the traditional value of tlawmngaihna (selfless service and putting others first) is an example of a value that guides behaviour and is learned through living in the community.
section-6: In the UHV framework, right understanding means understanding the harmony at all four levels of existence: within the human being, in the family, in society and in nature/existence. It is the first and most basic requirement for a fulfilling life.

Right understanding comes from within, through self-exploration, and not merely by memorizing information. With right understanding, a person can distinguish between what is truly needed and what is desired because of habit, advertising or peer pressure.
section-7: Relationships exist naturally: we are born into relationships with parents, siblings and relatives, and we develop other relationships with teachers, friends and colleagues. The course stresses that relationships are not created by us; we only need to understand and fulfil them.

The fulfilment of a relationship depends on the right feelings (values) such as trust and respect. When these feelings are present and expressed, both people feel happy; when they are absent, relationships become a source of conflict.
section-8: Physical facilities are needed to nourish, protect and use the body properly. They are needed in limited quantity, because the body's needs are limited. For example, a person can eat only a certain amount of food each day.

The course points out that physical facilities are necessary but not sufficient for human happiness. Animals need only physical facilities, but human beings also need right understanding and fulfilling relationships.
section-9: The three basic requirements are arranged in an order of priority: right understanding comes first, then relationship, and then physical facility. Right understanding helps us fulfil relationships and also helps us decide how much physical facility is needed.

When people focus only on physical facilities and neglect right understanding and relationships, they may become rich but remain unhappy. The course describes such a person as 'prosperous but unhappy'.
section-10: Self-exploration is described as a dialogue between 'what I am' and 'what I really want to be'. It involves looking at one's own desires, thoughts and behaviour and checking whether they are in harmony with what one truly wants.
Self-exploration is a process of self-evolution and self-investigation. It helps a person become more self-confident because decisions are based on one's own understanding.
section-11: The UHV course describes two mechanisms of self-exploration: natural acceptance and experiential validation. Natural acceptance means checking whether a proposal is naturally acceptable to us, that is, whether we want it from deep within, not because of fear, greed or habit. Experiential validation means testing the proposal in our behaviour and work to see whether it leads to mutual happiness and prosperity.

Natural acceptance is said to be constant (it does not change with time), universal (it is the same for all human beings) and innate. For example, everyone naturally accepts that being respected is better than being disrespected.
The content of self-exploration includes our basic aspirations ('What do I really want?') and the programme to fulfil them ('How can I achieve it?').
section-12: The course defines happiness as 'the state or situation in which I live, if there is harmony in it, I like to be in that state or situation'. Happiness is therefore being in harmony, and unhappiness is being in contradiction or conflict.

Excitement from sensual pleasure, new possessions or praise is often mistaken for happiness, but it is temporary. Continuous happiness comes from harmony within oneself and in relationships, and it does not depend only on external objects.
section-13: Prosperity is defined as 'the feeling of having or making available more than required physical facilities'. It involves two things: identifying the required quantity of physical facilities, and producing or obtaining more than that amount.

Prosperity is different from wealth. Wealth is the physical availability of money or goods, while prosperity is a feeling. A rich person who always feels that they need more is not prosperous, while a person with modest means who knows their needs and has enough can feel prosperous.
section-14: Every human being wants to be happy and to have that happiness continuously, together with prosperity. The course calls this the basic human aspiration.
To achieve this aspiration, a person needs right understanding, fulfilling relationships and adequate physical facilities, in that order of priority.
section-15: The course describes three typical situations. Some people lack physical facilities and are unhappy (deprived and unhappy). Some have physical facilities but are still unhappy (prosperous but unhappy). The goal is to be both happy and prosperous.

In the current scenario, the emphasis is mainly on accumulating physical facilities. This often leads to stress, competition, broken relationships, depression, crime and environmental damage. Many people believe that more wealth will automatically bring happiness, but experience shows that this is not true.
section-16: The programme to fulfil basic human aspirations is to understand the harmony at all four levels of existence and to live in harmony at all four levels: in the individual (the Self and the Body), in the family, in society, and in nature and existence.

Understanding comes first, and living according to that understanding follows. When a person lives in harmony, they experience continuous happiness, and when they produce more than they need, they experience prosperity.
section-18: There are two types of education: skill education ('how to do') and value education ('what to do'). The UHV course argues that both should be integrated, because skills without values can lead to misuse of knowledge, while values without skills cannot be implemented effectively.

The content of value education covers all levels of human existence: the individual, the family, society and nature/existence. It also covers all dimensions of human life, which are thought (realization and understanding), behaviour, work and participation in the larger order.

The importance of value education is seen in today's problems, such as stress, conflict in families, corruption, violence, addiction and environmental destruction. These problems arise not from a lack of skills or facilities but from a lack of right understanding.
Value education helps students to know themselves, to set the right goals in life, to build fulfilling relationships, to use technology responsibly and to contribute to a harmonious society.
section-19: Self-exploration means examining what is said in the course, as well as what one hears from others, instead of accepting or rejecting it without thinking. The student is asked to treat each idea as a proposal and to verify it on the basis of their own natural acceptance.

The process has two steps. The first is natural acceptance: is the proposal naturally acceptable to me? The second is experiential validation: when I live according to it, does it lead to happiness for me and others (in behaviour) and to prosperity (in work with nature)?
This method makes value education universal and non-sectarian, because it depends on each person's own verification and not on any particular religion, ideology or authority.
Through self-exploration, a person moves from 'assuming' and 'being influenced' to 'knowing' and 'being self-organized'. This leads to self-confidence, clarity and responsible living.
section-20: When asked what they want in life, people often name things like a good job, a big house, a car, or fame. If we ask why they want these things, the answer usually comes down to 'to be happy'. This shows that happiness is the basic aspiration, and the other things are means to it.

Happiness is a state of harmony, and its opposite is contradiction or conflict within oneself and with others. Physical facilities can satisfy the needs of the body, but they cannot give continuous happiness by themselves.

The course points out that the problem in today's world is that many people try to achieve happiness by accumulating physical facilities, which leads to a never-ending race. Prosperity is lost when one does not identify one's real needs.

Therefore, the course suggests the right programme: understand and live in harmony at all levels. With right understanding, relationships become fulfilling and the need for physical facilities becomes clear and limited, so both happiness and prosperity become possible.
section-21: Right understanding is needed by the Self ('I'), relationships are between one Self and another, and physical facilities are needed by the body. Each of these three requirements has a different role, and one cannot replace another.

Right understanding is the basis: it helps us understand relationships correctly and identify our needs for physical facilities. Without right understanding, we may try to buy respect through possessions or to fill emotional emptiness with consumption.
Relationships give mutual happiness when the right feelings are present. Physical facilities give a sense of prosperity when their required quantity is known and available.

A student can apply this by asking: Do I understand what I truly want? Are my relationships based on trust and respect? Do I know how much I really need? Answering these questions honestly is the first step towards a value-based life.
section-24: The course says that a human being is the co-existence of the sentient 'I' (the Self) and the material Body. 'I' is a conscious entity that has the activities of desiring, thinking and selecting/tasting, while the Body is a material entity that has physical and chemical activities such as breathing, digestion and heartbeat.
'I' is the seer, doer and enjoyer, while the Body is the instrument. For example, when I see a picture, the eyes are the instrument, but 'I' is the one who sees and understands.
section-25: The activities of the Self are continuous: desiring (imaging), thinking (analysing and comparing) and selecting/tasting (choosing what to do). These go on in 'I' all the time, even when the body is resting or asleep.
The Self is the source of feelings such as trust, respect, love and also of feelings such as fear, anger and jealousy. Understanding the Self is therefore essential for understanding human behaviour.
section-26: The Body is a self-organized unit made of cells, tissues and organs. It works on its own through activities like breathing, digestion and blood circulation, but it also responds to the Self's decisions, for example when we choose to walk or speak.
The Body needs nurturing (food, water, air), protection (clothing, shelter, medicine) and right utilization (using it for meaningful work).
section-27: The needs of 'I' are happiness (sukh) and right understanding. They are qualitative (they cannot be measured in quantity) and continuous (we want them all the time).
These needs are fulfilled by right understanding and right feelings, such as trust and respect in relationships, not by physical objects.
section-28: The needs of the Body are physical facilities (suvidha) such as food, clothing, shelter and medicine. They are quantitative (they can be measured) and temporary (once fulfilled, the need disappears for some time).
For example, after eating a full meal, the body does not need more food until it becomes hungry again. This shows that the body's needs are limited.
section-29: A comparison of the needs of I and the Body: the needs of I are happiness and right understanding, which are qualitative, continuous and fulfilled by right understanding and feelings. The needs of the Body are physical facilities, which are quantitative, temporary and fulfilled by physical and chemical things.

Problems arise when we try to fulfil the needs of I through physical facilities, for example trying to gain respect by buying expensive clothes or gadgets. This leads to unlimited wants and dissatisfaction.
section-30: The Self makes decisions and the Body carries them out. For example, I decide to read a book, and the eyes and hands help me do it. The Body itself does not decide; it is the instrument of 'I'.
Because the Body is an instrument, it is the responsibility of 'I' to take care of it, just as a skilled worker takes care of their tools.
section-31: Harmony in the Self means that the activities of desiring, thinking and selecting are in harmony with each other and with right understanding. When desires come from outside influences such as advertisements, peer pressure or habits, they may conflict with one another and create unhappiness.

When desires are based on right understanding and natural acceptance, there is no conflict within, and this inner harmony is experienced as happiness. The course calls this 'living with right understanding'.
section-32: Harmony of the Self with the Body means that 'I' understands the needs of the Body and takes care of it properly, and that the Body is used for meaningful purposes.

The course calls this 'sanyama' (self-regulation), which leads to 'swasthya' (health). Lack of harmony between the Self and the Body appears as overeating, lack of sleep, addiction, lack of exercise and neglect of hygiene.
section-33: Sanyama (self-regulation) is the feeling of responsibility in 'I' for nurturing, protecting and rightly utilizing the Body.

Nurturing means proper food, water and air. Protection means keeping the body safe through clothing, shelter, hygiene and treatment when needed. Right utilization means using the body for meaningful activities and not misusing it, for example through drugs, alcohol or overwork.
section-34: The course defines health (swasthya) as the condition in which the Body acts according to 'I' and its parts are in harmony with one another.

Health has physical, mental and social aspects. The World Health Organization defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'.
section-35: A programme for self-regulation and health includes eating balanced and timely meals, drinking clean water, getting enough sleep and rest, physical exercise or labour, yoga or breathing exercises, cleanliness and hygiene, avoiding harmful substances, and timely medical treatment.

The programme also includes the right use of the body in work and relationships. Students can practise self-regulation by planning a daily routine that balances study, rest, exercise and time with family and friends.
section-37: The human being is the co-existence of 'I' (the conscious Self) and the Body (the material part). 'I' is the seer, doer and enjoyer, while the Body is its instrument. This distinction is central to the whole course.

'I' and the Body differ in their needs, activities and nature. The needs of 'I' are happiness and right understanding, while the needs of the Body are physical facilities. The activities of 'I' are desiring, thinking and selecting, which are continuous, while the activities of the Body are physical and chemical processes such as breathing and digestion.

Many human problems arise because people confuse the needs of 'I' with the needs of the Body. For example, someone may try to feel respected or loved by buying luxury items, or try to escape inner conflict through alcohol or drugs. Such attempts fail because physical things cannot satisfy the needs of the Self.

Understanding the human being as the co-existence of the Self and the Body helps us give proper attention to both: right understanding and relationships for the Self, and right care and use for the Body.
section-38: The needs of 'I' are qualitative and continuous: we want happiness all the time, and its quality cannot be measured in kilograms or rupees. The needs of the Body are quantitative and temporary: they can be measured and are fulfilled for a time.

Because the Body's needs are limited, it is possible to identify the required quantity of physical facilities and to feel prosperous. The needs of 'I', however, cannot be fulfilled by physical facilities; they are fulfilled by right understanding and fulfilling relationships.

When people believe that the needs of 'I' can be met by physical facilities, their wants become unlimited. This leads to over-consumption, debt, competition, environmental destruction and unhappiness.
By clearly distinguishing the two kinds of needs, a person can use physical facilities wisely, avoid unnecessary consumption and focus on developing understanding and relationships.
section-39: 'I' is the decision-maker and the Body is the instrument that carries out decisions. The eyes see, the ears hear and the hands work, but it is 'I' that sees, hears, understands and decides.

The relationship between 'I' and the Body is one of responsibility. Just as a person takes care of a vehicle or a tool, 'I' must take care of the Body through proper nutrition, protection and right use.

When 'I' does not take responsibility, the Body suffers through neglect or misuse, for example through addiction, unhealthy eating, lack of sleep or overwork. When 'I' takes responsibility, the Body remains healthy and able to support meaningful work.
The idea of the Body as an instrument also means that the value of a person is not determined by physical appearance, but by the qualities of the Self.
section-40: Harmony in the Self means that desires, thoughts and selections are guided by right understanding. When desires come from external influences, such as advertisements or comparison with others, they often conflict with each other and create tension.

Harmony of the Self with the Body comes through sanyama (self-regulation), which means a feeling of responsibility for nurturing, protecting and rightly using the Body. Sanyama leads to swasthya (health), in which the Body works according to 'I' and its parts are in harmony.

A practical programme includes balanced food, regular exercise, enough rest, cleanliness, avoiding harmful substances and timely medical care. Yoga, walking, sports and manual work are useful forms of exercise.
In conclusion, inner harmony and physical health are connected. A person in inner conflict often neglects the body, while a person with right understanding takes care of the body naturally.
section-43: The family is the first place where a child learns about relationships, feelings and values. It is also the place where the human being first experiences trust, care and affection.

The course points out that the family is the basic unit of human order, and that harmony in the family is the basis for harmony in society. If there is harmony in each family, it can extend to the whole society.
section-44: Harmony in the family means living with right feelings in relationships and working together for prosperity. Each member understands their relationships and responsibilities and fulfils them.

The course identifies two parts of family harmony: mutual happiness in relationships (through trust, respect and other feelings) and prosperity in the family (through identifying needs and producing or earning more than needed together).
section-45: The course defines trust (vishwas) as 'to be assured that each human being inherently wants oneself and the other to be happy and prosperous'.

It distinguishes intention (what one wants to do) from competence (one's ability to do it). We often judge ourselves by our intention and others by their competence. If we recognize that others' intentions are also good, we can trust them even when their competence is lacking and help them improve.
Trust is called the foundational value because all other feelings in relationships depend on it.
section-46: Respect (samman) is defined as 'right evaluation'. Disrespect can take three forms: over-evaluation (evaluating someone as more than they are, such as flattering), under-evaluation (evaluating someone as less than they are, such as looking down on them) and otherwise-evaluation (evaluating someone as something else, such as judging them by caste or wealth).

Respect recognizes that the other person is similar to me in purpose (wanting continuous happiness), programme (understanding and living in harmony) and potential (the ability to achieve right understanding). Differences in body, wealth and position do not change this basic similarity.
section-47: The course lists nine feelings or values in relationships: trust (vishwas), respect (samman), affection (sneh), care (mamta), guidance (vatsalya), reverence (shraddha), glory (gaurav), gratitude (kritagyata) and love (prem).

Affection is the feeling of being related to the other. Care is the feeling of responsibility for nurturing and protecting the other's body. Guidance is the feeling of responsibility for ensuring right understanding in the other. Reverence is the acceptance of excellence in the other. Glory is the feeling for someone who has made efforts for excellence. Gratitude is the feeling towards those who have helped one achieve excellence. Love is the feeling of being related to all and is called the complete value.
section-48: The course defines justice (nyaya) in relationships as having four elements: recognition of values, fulfilment of values, right evaluation, and mutual happiness.

Justice starts in the family and extends to society. When justice is ensured in relationships, there is no exploitation or domination. Justice is not only legal justice provided by courts; it begins in everyday human relationships.
section-49: The course gives a 'comprehensive human goal' for harmony in society: right understanding in every individual, prosperity in every family, fearlessness (trust) in society and co-existence in nature.

To achieve this goal, the course identifies five dimensions of a human order: education and the inculcation of right values (shiksha-sanskar), health and self-regulation (swasthya-sanyama), production and work (utpadan-karya), justice and preservation (nyaya-suraksha), and exchange and storage (vinimay-kosh).
section-50: Universal human order (sarvabhaum vyavastha) is the idea that harmony can expand step by step from the family to the family cluster, the village, the nation and the whole world, forming a 'world family'.
This idea is similar to the ancient Indian ideal of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' ('the world is one family'). It suggests an 'undivided society' (akhand samaj) where all human beings are related.
section-51: Nature is made up of countless units, each of which is self-organized and connected with others. Examples are a stone, a tree, a bird and a human being.

The course says that all units exist in 'space', which is all-pervasive, and that existence is the co-existence of units in space. Understanding this helps human beings see themselves as part of nature, not separate from it.
section-52: Every unit in nature is related to every other unit. For example, plants take minerals from the soil, animals depend on plants, and human beings depend on soil, plants and animals.
Examples include the water cycle, the carbon cycle and food chains, which show how everything is connected.
section-53: Nature is self-regulated: it maintains its own balance. Forests regulate rainfall, the number of animals is controlled by the availability of food and predators, and soil fertility is maintained by decaying leaves and organisms.

Human beings are the only order that can disturb this balance through over-exploitation, pollution and deforestation. Therefore, humans have a special responsibility to understand and support self-regulation in nature.
section-54: Mutual fulfilment means that the material order, plant order and animal order naturally fulfil each other. For example, plants enrich the soil, animals help in pollination and seed dispersal, and decaying matter returns nutrients to the soil.
Human beings should also be mutually fulfilling to the other orders, by using resources responsibly, recycling, conserving and protecting the environment.
section-55: The four orders are: the material order (padarth avastha), such as soil, water, metals and air; the plant or bio order (pran avastha), such as grass, trees and microorganisms; the animal order (jeev avastha), such as birds, cattle and fish; and the human order (gyan avastha), human beings.

The course describes each order in terms of things, activity, innateness, natural characteristic and basic guideline. For example, the natural characteristic of the human order is described as perseverance, bravery and generosity (dhirata, virata and udarata).

Each later order includes the earlier ones: the plant order contains material, the animal order contains plant and material, and the human order contains all three, while also possessing the ability to understand.
section-57: The family is the first school of relationships. Harmony in the family requires understanding of relationships and right feelings, especially trust and respect, along with working together for prosperity.

Trust is the foundational value. The course explains that trust means being assured that the other person also wants me to be happy and prosperous. We usually judge ourselves by our intention but others by their competence, which leads to mistrust. When we see that the other person's intention is also good, we can trust them and help them improve their competence.
Mistrust leads to fear, suspicion, conflicts and the breakdown of relationships. Trust leads to openness, cooperation and mutual happiness.
Family harmony is the basis for harmony in society. A child who grows up in a family with trust and respect is more likely to extend these feelings to others.
section-58: Respect is right evaluation. It is not just politeness, flattery or fear. True respect recognizes that the other person is similar to me in purpose, programme and potential.

Disrespect takes three forms: over-evaluation (praising someone more than they deserve), under-evaluation (thinking someone is less than they are) and otherwise-evaluation (judging someone by something other than what they are, such as their caste, religion, gender, wealth or appearance).
Discrimination based on caste, gender, race, religion or wealth is an example of otherwise-evaluation and is the cause of many social problems. Right evaluation leads to equality and dignity.
Respect also means recognizing differences in competence and helping each other to develop. A teacher respects a student by recognizing the student's potential and guiding them.
section-59: Justice in human relationships has four elements: recognition of values (knowing what the relationship is and what feelings it requires), fulfilment of values (expressing those feelings in behaviour), right evaluation (checking whether feelings were properly fulfilled) and mutual happiness (the result that both feel happy).
Justice starts in the family. When justice is not ensured in families, injustice spreads to society, leading to exploitation, domination and conflict.

The nine feelings in relationships — trust, respect, affection, care, guidance, reverence, glory, gratitude and love — form the content of justice. Love, the feeling of being related to all, is the complete value.
Legal justice is needed when there is a breakdown, but the course argues that true justice must begin with right understanding in relationships.
section-60: The course states the comprehensive human goal as right understanding in every individual, prosperity in every family, fearlessness (trust) in society and co-existence in nature.

The human order to achieve this goal has five dimensions: education and right values (shiksha-sanskar), health and self-regulation (swasthya-sanyama), production and work (utpadan-karya), justice and preservation (nyaya-suraksha), and exchange and storage (vinimay-kosh).
The universal human order develops from the family to the family cluster, the village, the region, the nation and the world. This is similar to the ideal of 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'.

In this order, systems are based on right understanding and mutual happiness, not on fear, domination or competition. The course argues that this is a realistic goal if each individual and family begins with right understanding.
section-61: The four orders of nature are the material order (soil, water, air, metals), the plant or bio order (plants and trees), the animal order (animals and birds) and the human order (human beings). Each higher order includes the lower orders.

The material, plant and animal orders are mutually fulfilling: they support each other naturally. For example, plants take nutrients from the soil and return them through decaying leaves; animals feed on plants and help in pollination.

Human beings are the only order that is not yet mutually fulfilling, because of a lack of right understanding. Over-exploitation of resources, deforestation, pollution and climate change show the harm caused by human behaviour.

With right understanding, human beings can become mutually fulfilling with all orders by using resources responsibly, conserving forests, recycling waste and choosing sustainable lifestyles. In Mizoram, community forest reserves and efforts to reduce jhum burning are examples of ways to support harmony with nature.
section-64: Holistic understanding means understanding harmony at all four levels — the individual, family, society and nature/existence — and seeing how they are connected.
With holistic understanding, a person sees that personal choices about consumption, work and relationships affect family, society and nature.
section-65: In the UHV approach, professional ethics means the ability to use one's professional competence for the fulfilment of the comprehensive human goal, that is, for mutual happiness and prosperity.

Codes of conduct exist in many professions, such as medicine, law, engineering, teaching and journalism, but the course argues that ethical behaviour must come from right understanding, not only from external rules.
section-66: The course says that ethical human conduct is definite (definitive) when it is based on right understanding. Without right understanding, a person's behaviour may change depending on circumstances, fear or greed.

Definitive ethical conduct includes values in relationships (trust, respect), policy (to enrich, protect and use resources rightly) and character (chastity in conjugal relations, rightful earning and kindness in behaviour).
section-67: Humanistic education aims to develop right understanding together with professional skills. It helps students become responsible human beings and responsible professionals.
The course suggests that value education should be included in all education, from school to higher education, so that knowledge and skills are used for human welfare.
section-68: A humanistic constitution is described as a constitution based on right understanding and the comprehensive human goal. It would ensure that systems such as education, health, production, justice and exchange are designed to promote mutual happiness and prosperity.
The Indian Constitution, with its values of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity in the Preamble, provides a foundation for such humanistic values.
section-69: Universal human order in professional life means that professions contribute to the five dimensions of human order and to the well-being of all.

For example, a doctor contributes to health, a teacher to education, an engineer to production, a lawyer to justice and a banker to exchange. When each profession works with right understanding, together they create a harmonious society.
section-70: The course says that competence in professional ethics includes: the ability to utilize professional competence to augment universal human order; the ability to identify the scope and characteristics of people-friendly and eco-friendly production systems; the ability to identify and develop appropriate technologies and management patterns; and the ability to work with others to develop such systems.
Ethical competence also includes clarity about the comprehensive human goal, confidence in oneself and others, and the ability to resist unethical pressures.
section-71: The course lists criteria for holistic technologies: they should cater to real human needs, be compatible with natural systems and cycles, be eco-friendly and people-friendly, and ensure effective use of local resources and human ingenuity.
Examples include solar and wind energy, rainwater harvesting, organic farming, biogas plants, energy-efficient buildings, recycling technologies and appropriate local technologies.
section-72: The course suggests that production systems should be cyclic (like natural systems), mutually enriching (both for humans and nature), and based on decentralized, local production where possible.

Mass production and consumerism often lead to waste, pollution and the exploitation of workers. Value-based production systems aim at producing what is needed, with minimum waste and maximum benefit for people and nature.
section-73: Value-based management models emphasize participatory decision-making, fair treatment of workers, transparency, social responsibility and long-term sustainability, not only short-term profit.

Examples include cooperative enterprises (such as Amul), self-help groups and businesses that practise corporate social responsibility. Under the Companies Act, 2013, certain companies in India must spend part of their profits on corporate social responsibility (CSR) activities.
section-74: The transition to a value-based life begins with self-exploration and continues with gradual changes in thought, behaviour and work. It is a step-by-step process, not a sudden change.
Practical steps include reflecting on one's needs, reducing wasteful consumption, improving relationships through trust and respect, taking care of health and contributing to society and nature.
section-75: Transition towards a value-based profession means using one's professional skills for human welfare and refusing to engage in unethical practices such as corruption, cheating and exploitation.
Professionals can contribute by choosing ethical employers, developing eco-friendly products, being honest with clients, mentoring younger colleagues and participating in community service.
section-77: Holistic understanding means understanding the harmony at all levels of existence: within oneself, in the family, in society and in nature. Professional activity is a part of this whole and is connected to all levels.

Professional ethics in the UHV approach is not a separate set of rules; it is the natural result of right understanding. A person with right understanding will use their professional competence to promote mutual happiness and prosperity.

Unethical practices in professions, such as corruption, medical negligence, adulteration of food, environmental pollution and misleading advertising, arise from a lack of right understanding and from the belief that wealth alone brings happiness.
The course suggests that ethical professionals contribute to the comprehensive human goal: right understanding in individuals, prosperity in families, trust in society and co-existence in nature.
section-78: The course describes ethical human conduct as definite when it is based on right understanding rather than on fear, greed or external pressure. Such conduct is consistent across situations.

Definitive human conduct has three components: values (trust, respect and other feelings in relationships), policy (enrichment, protection and right utilization of resources), and character (rightful earning, chastity in conjugal relations and kindness in behaviour).
In professional life, this means honesty, fairness, accountability, transparency, respect for colleagues and clients, and concern for the environment and society.
Ethics then becomes part of professional excellence. A good professional is not only skilled but also trustworthy and responsible.
section-79: Humanistic education combines right understanding with professional skills. It produces individuals who are not only employable but also responsible citizens and human beings.

A humanistic constitution would be based on right understanding and would aim at the comprehensive human goal. The Indian Constitution, with its ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, already reflects many humanistic values.

Universal human order is the vision of a society in which harmony spreads from the individual and family to the whole world. The five dimensions of human order — education, health, production, justice and exchange — work together to support it.
In conclusion, education, constitution and social order must all be grounded in human values for a harmonious society.
section-80: Competence in professional ethics, according to the UHV course, includes the ability to use professional competence to augment universal human order; the ability to identify people-friendly and eco-friendly production systems; the ability to develop appropriate technologies and management patterns; and the ability to work collaboratively.
It also includes clarity about the comprehensive human goal, confidence in one's own values and the courage to resist unethical pressure.

Examples: an engineer who designs energy-efficient products, a doctor who prescribes only necessary treatment, an accountant who refuses to falsify accounts, and a teacher who treats every student with respect.
Such competence must be developed through education, reflection and practice, and is as important as technical skills.
section-81: Holistic technologies cater to real human needs, are compatible with natural cycles, are eco-friendly and people-friendly, and make effective use of local resources. Examples include solar energy, rainwater harvesting, organic farming and recycling.
Value-based production systems should be cyclic and mutually enriching, producing what is needed with minimum waste. They should avoid overproduction and over-consumption.

Value-based management models include participatory management, cooperatives, self-help groups and enterprises committed to social responsibility. They aim at the well-being of workers, consumers, society and nature.
The transition from profit-centred to value-based systems requires changes in thinking, education, policies and consumer choices.
section-82: At the level of the individual, the transition involves self-exploration, developing right understanding and practising self-regulation for health.
At the level of the family and society, it involves building relationships based on trust, respect and justice, and contributing to community welfare.
At the level of profession, it involves using skills ethically, choosing holistic technologies and supporting value-based production and management.

Strategies include value education in curricula, faculty development, role models, institutional policies that reward ethical conduct, and community participation. The course argues that this transition is gradual but achievable, beginning with each individual.
section-83: A useful way to revise is to remember the four levels of harmony: the individual (Self and Body), the family (relationships), society (universal human order) and nature (four orders and co-existence). Professional ethics is the application of this understanding in work.

Key terms to remember are natural acceptance, experiential validation, happiness, prosperity, sanyama, swasthya, trust, respect, justice, the comprehensive human goal, the five dimensions of human order and the four orders of nature.
